overview:
Russia in the autumn of 1917 was a state that had already lost one government and was failing to sustain a second. The February revolution had swept away the Romanov monarchy, leaving a Provisional Government that shared authority uneasily with the soviets — councils of workers, soldiers and sailors — and that insisted on staying in a war whose casualties, food shortages and desertions were pulling the country apart. Through the summer the Bolsheviks, a faction of Russian Marxists led by Vladimir Lenin, moved from the fringe to majorities in the Petrograd and Moscow soviets on a programme of peace, land and soviet power. On the night of 24–25 October by the old Russian calendar — 6–7 November in the Western one, which is why an October revolution is now marked in November — Red Guards and pro-Bolshevik soldiers occupied the capital's railway stations, telegraph offices, bridges and power stations. The Provisional Government's ministers, sitting in the Winter Palace with a thin guard of cadets, Cossacks and a women's battalion, held out until roughly two in the morning before insurgents entered and arrested them; Alexander Kerensky had already fled the city.

The seizure was less a battle than an administrative takeover with rifles, and it is worth being blunt about the gap between what happened and how it was later pictured. The eyewitness accounts describe an improvised, uneven affair with grenades thrown at a door, a handful of wounded cadets and negligible resistance — not the surging human wave of Soviet iconography, which owes more to a mass re-enactment staged in Petrograd in 1920 and to Sergei Eisenstein's 1928 film than to October 1917. Bolshevik forces in the capital numbered perhaps twenty to thirty thousand. Moscow, where fighting ran for a week, was far bloodier. The Second All-Russian Congress of Soviets, meeting as the palace fell, ratified the new government and issued decrees on peace and on land, and the moderate socialists who walked out in protest left the field to Lenin's party.

Holding power proved much harder than taking it. Elections to a Constituent Assembly in November returned a Socialist Revolutionary plurality rather than a Bolshevik one, and the assembly was dissolved by force after a single day in January 1918. The armistice with the Central Powers and the punitive Treaty of Brest-Litovsk in March 1918 bought peace at the cost of vast western territories, and the collapse of the old imperial army into rival national and political formations spread violence far beyond Petrograd. The fighting around Bobruysk in Belarus in the winter of 1918, where General Józef Dowbor-Muśnicki's Polish I Corps refused a Soviet order to disband and clashed with the new Red Army before coming to terms with advancing German troops, is one small instance of that unravelling — and of how quickly a night in one capital became a civil war across a continent-sized country.
significance: October 1917 produced the first state anywhere to be founded on an avowedly Marxist programme, and the institutions improvised in its first months — a single ruling party, a political police, government by decree, land and industry taken into state hands — became the template that reshaped Russia and, after 1945, much of Eurasia and beyond. It gave the twentieth century one of its organising antagonisms, splitting the international socialist movement permanently between communists and social democrats, supplying anticolonial movements from China to Cuba with both a model and a patron, and giving conservative and fascist politics across Europe a mobilising fear. It also became one of history's most contested precedents: an argument, still unresolved, about whether a determined minority seizing a state in a moment of collapse is a revolution or a coup, and about how much of what followed — the civil war, the famines, the terror — was already implied in that night.
coverage: Written from the linked reference works plus Ohio State's Origins essay, an eyewitness account of the Winter Palace hosted by Michigan State's Seventeen Moments in Soviet History, and the 1914–1918-Online entry on Polish units in Russia. The dataset holds only two events here — the Winter Palace and a 1918 clash at Bobruysk that actually sits outside the 1917 span — so nothing beneath this story covers Lenin's return, the July Days, the Kornilov affair, the Second Congress of Soviets, the week of fighting in Moscow, or events outside the capitals, which is where most Russians experienced 1917. The record itself is also unusually filtered: Soviet historiography retrofitted the night into an epic for seventy years, hostile émigré accounts pulled the other way, and although post-1991 archive access has settled much of the factual detail, participant numbers, casualties and the depth of popular support remain genuinely disputed.
